01 case-study · multi-shipping-options

Patients kept walking out the door. We gave them a reason to stay.

uMeds delivers medication to patients across Australia. But every month, around a thousand of them asked to take their script elsewhere. This is the story of why, what we built about it, and the honest result: a 19% drop in patient-initiated churn, an estimated $13.7M a year protected, and two launch targets we missed.

why

Standard delivery didn't fit how patients wanted their medication. So they left.

how

Research with real patients, then a shipping experience built around choice and trust.

what

Same-day, weekend, 3-hour and click-and-collect, shipped inside the existing flow.

role
Scoping, research, interaction design, prototyping, testing, stakeholder management, change management and post-implementation tracking
timeline
Research Q2 2025 → launch Nov 2025 → continuous review Jun 2026
surface
uMeds B2C ordering & checkout (web)

case-study · multi-shipping-options

The short version

Patients were leaving because standard delivery did not fit how they wanted their medication. We gave them more ways to receive it. It missed both launch targets as written, yet cut patient-initiated churn 19% and protected an estimated $13.7M a year in a declining market. Size the market before you set the metric.

before · the world we were in

Every month, about 1,050 patients asked to leave.

When a patient requests a script release, they take their prescription to a pharmacy themselves instead of ordering through uMeds. We were not guessing why. Patients told us, in two datasets.

Why patients requested a script release

I wanted to pick up in person59% I needed it urgently27.5% I had delivery issues before20.3% I preferred a pharmacy I know19.4% Lower prices elsewhere10.4% Ordering process was difficult9.2% Other6.9%

source: Survicate discharge survey (script-release reasons)

What shipping options patients actually wanted

Shipping offers / discounts5,524 Same day delivery4,360 Weekend delivery3,469 Delivery within 3 hours2,067 Click-and-collect1,984 None of these1,270 Other580

source: Google Looker, uMeds Post Delivery NPS, CSat & Awaiting Collection / Delivery Attempted

59% just wanted to pick up in person. The demand was specific: same-day (4,360), weekend (3,469), 3-hour (2,067) and click-and-collect (1,984). Doing nothing meant keeping the leak open.

after · imagine the alternative

A patient notices their medication is running low. They open uMeds and, for the first time, they actually have a choice: same-day if it's urgent, collect it nearby, or pick a day that suits them. The reason to walk out the door is gone.

That is the world we were designing toward. Not a faster version of the old experience, but a genuinely different one, where how the medication arrives bends to the patient instead of the other way around.

bridge · how we got there

First understand the patient, then design for trust, not just speed.

I ran moderated, task-based usability sessions with seven patients on a prototype of the new shipping experience. The sample leans rural, the group with the most to gain and the least margin for a failed delivery.

participantsegmentnotable context
Participant 1MetroOnly uses mobile and wants the quickest option
Participant 2RuralWould drive ~50 km to collect if an item is unavailable locally
Participant 3RuralOrders on a laptop; found the mobile screen confusing
Participant 4RuralChose SDD over 3-hour for a marginal cost saving
Participant 5RuralRanks speed lowest, behind quality, value and cost
Participant 6MetroAvoids click-and-collect over personal-safety concerns
Participant 7RuralLeans on SMS / AusPost alerts to track orders

The scorecard told me where the design would struggle

passedSelect a shipping option✓ Finds the section, reads each option, picks the one that matches intent

partialConfirm availability & present valid ID✕ A patient questioned a "valid ID" banner on a standard express order

failedUnderstand availability based on location✕ Could not tell which options were available vs unavailable, with drop-off risk

What patients said

The three ideas that shaped the design

  1. 01

    Make availability legible

    Greyed-out options read as noise. Patients need to see what their address actually supports, or a faster option silently disappears.

  2. 02

    Match trust cues to the choice

    An ID banner on a standard order broke trust. Verification messaging has to be conditional on the option chosen.

  3. 03

    Design for control, not just speed

    Rural patients rank speed below value and reliability. The win is choice, not raw velocity.

The screen those ideas became

Choice up front

Same-day, standard and collect sit side by side, each leading with price and a plain-language ETA.

Conditional trust

The valid-ID acknowledgement appears only on the option that needs it.

Honest availability

The biggest open problem from testing: unavailable options must read as unavailable, not greyed out. Recreation shown; product name masked in the design itself.

cross-functional delivery

A shipping option in the UI is a chain of real-world handoffs behind it

Choosing "Same Day" looks like a single tap. Underneath it triggers a tightly timed, regulated chain: a serviceability check, a script and ID compliance step, a dispense within the cut-off window, a pick-and-pack, a courier collection, a same-day route and a status message back to the patient. No single team owns that chain end-to-end, which is exactly where it can break.

Before a pixel was finalised, I ran a cross-functional mapping workshop with Fulfilment, Pharmacy Operations, Delivery, Engineering, Data and Marketing/Comms. The goal was deliberately not "review my designs" it was to build one shared map of the operation so every user scenario, edge case, risk and dependency had a named owner, and so the design decisions in checkout reflected what operations could actually honour. The output was the workshopped IxD process map below.

Scenarios & risks the workshop put on the table

Mapping the operation together surfaced the cross-cutting scenarios a checkout mock alone would never expose each one now had an owner and a fallback rather than becoming a live incident:

01

Cut off missed

Order placed after the same-day dispatch window. Who downgrades the option, and how is the patient told before they pay?

02

Out-of-zone after address change

A faster option silently drops when the address updates (the shipping option friction) engineering recompute plus a visible message, owned jointly.

03

Script not yet released

Pharmacy can't dispense until the script clears. Comms holds the SMS rather than promising a window that can't be met.

04

Stock mismatch

Online availability disagrees with the shelf. Fulfilment feeds live stock into eligibility so SDD never shows for an item that isn't there.

05

Cold-chain item

Temperature-sensitive products constrain packing and carrier. This flagged at eligibility, not discovered at pick.

06

Failed delivery / re-attempt

Re-attempt logic, PTX followup and proactive comms agreed up front, so a missed drop doesn't read to the patient as a lost order.

The wider point: I treat what happens after handoff as part of the design. Getting Fulfilment, Pharmacy, Delivery, Engineering, Data and Marketing Comms aligned on one map is what turned a clean shipping options flow into a promise the product team could keep and it's also where the eligible-market blind spot behind Target 1 first became visible.

what · what we shipped, and what it did

More ways to receive medication. Two missed targets. One real win.

Same Day Delivery (SDD) launched in November 2025, with Click & Collect (CC) following in March 2026. Against the two launch targets the literal numbers are a miss. Against the thing that mattered, retention, it is a clear win.

missedTarget 1: 25% SDD conversion

Result: 8.5% by May 2026, peaking at 10.8% in Feb.

  • The 25% was set against all orders, before sizing how many were even SDD-eligible.
  • Greyed-out options were unreadable, so eligible patients sometimes missed SDD.

missedTarget 2: +1.5% total order uplift

Result: −6.6% market-wide, but the no-SDD control fell −19.3% like-for-like; SDD adopters held at +0.6%, beating the market by about 15 points.

The targets measured new growth. What SDD actually delivered was retention.

SDD adoption vs the 25% target

Peak share, Feb 2026
SDD-enabled postcodesBlended (all orders)25% target

Measured on all orders, adoption peaked at 10.8%. On SDD-eligible postcodes (illustrative, ~40% of orders) it tracks near the 25% target.

Patient-initiated churn −19%

Monthly average

Revenue / customer / 30d

By segment vs baseline
Baseline$253 S1$196 S2$299 S3$152
−19%

+$147

0.55%

so what · what I'd carry forward

A success metric is only as good as the market definition under it.

01

Recalibrate the target

Re-base SDD conversion on SDD-eligible orders, not all orders.

02

Fix availability legibility

Remove or clearly explain unavailable options instead of greying them out.

03

Make option changes loud

When an address change drops a faster option, say so.

04

Lead with retention

Frame SDD around churn protection and multi-modal value, not raw adoption.

case study · 2021 · double diamond · award winning

Changing the way young Australians bank

A youth banking experience for Westpac, designed to attract 12 to 18 year olds and turn first accounts into lifelong money habits. I led the research and design across a 3-week sprint.

role
Team lead, UX research and design
team
Remote team Westpac
timeline
3 weeks, April 2021
target
+10% new youth customers

case study · 2021 · double diamond · award winning

The short version

A 200-year-old bank was losing the next generation. Through research with 60+ young people and a co-designed, tested product, we shipped a goal-based first slice: Savings Goals for your child, where parents assign tasks to earn money toward the goal, a visual progress tracker, a confetti finish and savings on autopilot. Aimed at a 10% lift in new youth customers and healthier money habits for life, then held the rest of the flows for post-implementation research.

Canstar's Outstanding Value for Junior & Youth Banking 2024-2026
WeMoney Winner 2025 for Youth Account of the Year

the challenge

A 200-year-old bank young people had no reason to choose.

Westpac opened more than 200 years ago as the Bank of New South Wales, the first bank in Australia. Two centuries on, it captured millennials well but barely registered with the generation behind them.

Working with product managers, creative strategists and UX/UI designers, we set out to attract a youth segment for a projected 10% uplift in new customers. Every element had to carry the brand promise: Westpac is remarkably helpful, in life's moments big and small.

discover

Understand a generation the bank had never researched.

I led the research with a clear framework: a 5 C's analysis, a SWOT, a competitor review, 18 one-to-one interviews and 60 young people aged 12 to 18 informing the work. A few findings that shaped everything: 59% had hit money worries, most parents banked with CBA or ANZ, and Gen Z favours bite-sized, expressive, social content.

What young people told us

How do you receive this money?

57 responses · free text, multiple answers possible
Allowance24 · 42.1% Job17 · 29.8% Gifts10 · 17.5% Parents2 · 3.5% I don't2 · 3.5% Other free-text8 · 1.8% ea

The tail of single answers told the real story: parents when I ask, youth allowance (Centrelink), working for parent, chores, and don't get any.

Do you have a bank account? Who opened it?

57 responses
  • Parent or guardian opened it54.4%
  • Opened it myself26.3%
  • Don't have one19.3%

How much money do you receive each week?

57 responses
  • Less than $5063.2%
  • $51 to $10022.8%
  • $200+8.8%
  • $101 to $1505.2%

Where does any money you have or earn usually go?

31 responses
  • Into my piggy bank at home41.9%
  • Straight into my bank account38.7%
  • Other: parents' account, invest, pocket, wallet, a mix, n/a19.4%

Even among savers, nearly half still kept cash in a piggy bank rather than a usable account. The opportunity was to make the bank the obvious, rewarding home for their money.

define

Three people, one shared need: money that feels manageable.

Sophie

17 · student, part-time at Woolworths

Juggling school and work, motivated to move out of home soon, and will need help managing a tighter budget if she cuts her hours.

Liam

14 · student, no job yet, introverted

Overwhelmed balancing hobbies and homework, wants a faster way to save for the latest gaming tech and keep up with friends.

Emily

43 · parent of two, the household budgeter

Time-poor but family-focused, she wants a simple way to support her kids' financial goals and worries about their future.

How might we

HMW 01

Win the youth market

Attract 10% more customers in the youth segment.

HMW 02

Help Sophie cope

Manage her money through high school and still enjoy life's moments.

HMW 03

Help Liam & Emily

Track money, work toward a goal, and celebrate reaching it.

develop

From a hundred ideas to a minimum viable product.

I facilitated a remote co-design workshop for Westpac, on Miro. We ran Crazy 8's, then voted features on a high-value, low-effort quadrant. The features fell into six categories.

01

Tasks

Simple to-dos that build money habits.

02

Mailbox & notifications

Timely nudges, surfaced on the homepage.

03

Customizability

Self-expression with characters and emojis.

04

Rewards hub

Wins and incentives that keep momentum.

05

Digiwallet

Everyday payments, expenses and budgeting.

06

Goals

Visible targets to save toward.

Low-fidelity wireframes

From the voted features and user flows, I built low-fidelity wireframes for the core screens, then expanded them into mid-fidelity as a team.

deliver · what shipped

A goal-based youth bank, shipped to production.

shipped

Set up Savings Goals for your child

A parent creates a goal, sets the amount and date, then assigns tasks the child completes to earn money toward it. Pocket money becomes a shared goal.

shipped

A visual goal progress tracker

An outer ring shows how much is saved, an inner ring shows time elapsed, so young savers see at a glance whether they are on track.

shipped

A confetti moment at the finish line

Reaching a goal triggers a burst of confetti and a warm prompt to set a new target. A small celebration that makes saving feel worth it.

shipped

Savings on autopilot

Schedule recurring transfers to each goal every pay day, with tips on how much you can realistically afford to save.

+12 pt

Illustrative post-launch signals, representative of the early read. The formal post-implementation study was the agreed next step.

Years later...

The youth savers goals initiative went on to win rewards.

Canstar's Outstanding Value

for Junior & Youth Banking 2024-2026

what's next

We shipped the loop that mattered, then stopped to learn.

Held out of scope, on purpose

  • The full wallet, payments and cards.
  • Account opening and parental consent at scale.
  • A broader rewards marketplace.
  • Social and expressive features the co-design surfaced.

Pending post-implementation research

  • Run the formal study to confirm the signals.
  • Test friction in goal setup and the parent-task loop.
  • Measure whether the habit holds past the first goal.
  • Use the findings to refine, then expand the flows once the youth market is proven.

case study · 2024 · internal admin tooling

Redesigning Circuit, the portal that runs Montu's operations

Circuit is the internal admin portal Montu's operations teams use to manage orders, patients, approvals and pharmacies. It had grown for years without evolving. I led the research to find where it was failing the people who live in it, and set a direction grounded in evidence.

role
UX research lead, UX design
users
PTX, PharmOps and Clinical (RN) teams
timeline
Discovery from Nov 2024, phased to v1.2
my focus
Research, synthesis, design direction, MUI

case study · 2024 · internal admin tooling

The short version

Circuit was a legacy admin portal that grew without evolving. I led discovery and usability research with ten people across cross functional teams (PTX, PharmOps and Clinical), ran a heuristic and accessibility review of every core screen, and turned it into a workflow-first redesign on the Montu MUI design system. v1.2 lifted satisfaction on every core screen from below the line to between 4.6-5 out of 5.

the problem

It grew, but it never evolved.

Circuit started with an external agency that had limited business context. Over the years, features were layered on top of features, a frankenstein build stitched together by whoever needed the next thing shipped.

It worked, technically, but fought the people using it. Designs were added without validating user needs, workflows were disjointed, and with no cohesive standards every new screen drifted further from the last.

01

No user-centred design

Designs were outsourced and functionality was added without validating user needs or doing research.

02

Disjointed workflows

Ad-hoc additions left the PTX team navigating a fragmented portal with manual steps and multiple open tabs.

03

Usability and design gaps

With no cohesive standards, inconsistencies piled up and dragged on usability and productivity.

methodology

A research-led approach, from discovery to validation.

discovery research

Understand the work

Semi-structured interviews, contextual inquiry to observe real usage, and a Pre-Post improvement score to set a baseline.

usability testing

Validate the redesign

Task-based testing on real scenarios like flagging orders and AP/SAS approvals, a think-aloud protocol, and prototype testing.

analysis & collaboration

Synthesise and align

Thematic analysis, the Pre-Post score, peer reviews, and prioritisation workshops with delivery and product against OKRs.

Who I spoke to

04PTX (Patient Experience)03PharmOps03Clinical (RNs)

heuristic review

I also pulled the interface apart, screen by screen.

Alongside the user sessions, I ran an expert heuristic evaluation of every core Circuit screen, scored each issue against usability heuristics and Gestalt principles, checked accessibility, and tagged it by the fix it needed. All documented on Confluence for stakeholder visibility.

How I did it

  • Walked the four core surfaces one by one: Orders list, Order details, Patients list and Pharmacies.
  • Evaluated each against usability heuristics and Gestalt principles like similarity and proximity.
  • Ran automated accessibility audits with WebAIM WAVE for contrast, focus and semantic-markup issues.
  • Tagged every issue by category and by the fix it needed: improvement, rewrite or redesign.
  • Backed each finding with annotated screenshots and sketched concept redesigns.

What it surfaced

Ambiguous tables and labels

Headings that did not say what they meant (one "Date" for payment, order or shipping), unlabelled icons, and unrelated controls side by side.

Broken responsiveness

Tables and the header did not scale, cutting off data when the window was resized.

Hidden, unexpected behaviour

Users had to clear the search field to see orders, filters worked one at a time, and the page went blank when filters were removed.

Accessibility debt

Around 150 errors across the core screens, plus missing focus states, low contrast and link colours failing WCAG.

Drift from the design system

Buttons, hovers and layouts were inconsistent with the Montu MUI design system.

104
Orders list

automated accessibility errors

21
Patients list

automated accessibility errors

18
Order details

missing form-label errors

7

automated accessibility errors

source: Circuit heuristic review with WebAIM WAVE, 2024

what I heard

Four themes ran through everything.

Data visibility and integration

A lack of integration with the pharmacy system forced manual tracking of approvals, cancellations and dosage. Fragmented data made compliance hard to follow.

Usability and navigation

Unintuitive filters, excessive scrolling and inconsistent layouts created friction, and search was limited by identifiers.

Workflow efficiency

Tracking, flagging and reallocating orders meant manual steps and multiple tabs, with no order flagging, status history or bulk actions.

Compliance challenges

AP and SAS approval handling was cumbersome and error-prone without visibility, so people tracked rules in external spreadsheets.

The baseline, before any redesign

I captured a Pre score on a five-point scale across the core screens. Every screen sat below the line.

source: Pre-Post improvement score, Circuit usability research, Nov 2024

the direction

A phased redesign, focused on workflow first.

The findings pointed to one priority: give the operations teams back their time. The work was sequenced into phases, with the first features aimed at workflow efficiency on a consistent MUI design system.

workflow

Duplicate, order flagging, status history and bulk actions

The tools people kept asking for. Duplicate, flag and track orders, see a clear status history, and act on many orders at once instead of one tab at a time.

shipped

Search the way people actually work

Find patients and orders by the identifiers used day to day, including patient ID, with simplified tables that lead with the most important information.

shipped

Approvals with visibility built in

Bring AP and SAS approval handling into Circuit with the visibility and structure that used to live in spreadsheets, reducing human error.

shipped

One consistent design system

A shared MUI-based design system so every screen is consistent by default, ending the drift that caused the usability gaps.

A selected list of four highly requested screens and flows that allow internal users to finish their jobs and reduce human errors. Sensitive information is all redacted and placeholder information is displayed.

how we measure it · v1.2 results

Every core screen moved, and moved a lot.

I re-ran the same Pre-Post improvement score on the v1.2 redesign, rebuilt on the Montu MUI design system, with the same teams. Satisfaction on every core screen climbed from below the line into the 4.6 to 5.0 range.

What users said about v1.2

data visibility

Clear at a glance

10 of 10 found the layout clean and clear, and 9 of 10 said it gave enough information for a faster workflow.

usability

Less hunting

8 of 10 had less scrolling and better filters, and 10 of 10 liked the intuitive search and new patient ID search.

workflow

Real time savers

10 of 10 loved copy-to-clipboard, and 10 of 10 valued the Status History Log showing what changed, when and by whom.

compliance

Approvals in view

All 3 clinical users liked the new SAS approval and upload UI, and 10 of 10 liked the clearer remaining units and repeats.

operational impact

The satisfaction lift is really time handed back to the team.

The features users rated highest, bulk actions, status history, copy-to-clipboard and faster search, all attack the same thing: the manual steps, extra tabs and side spreadsheets between a PTX agent and a finished task. Modelled against the workflow that shipped, the saving compounds quickly.

~40%
Faster on key tasks

Search, flagging, reallocating and approvals.

~1 hr
Saved per agent, per day

Fewer manual steps, tabs and lookups.

~6,000 hrs
Saved a year

Across the PTX team, conservatively.

~3 FTE
Capacity reinvested

Freed to handle more, without hiring.

modelled estimate from the usability findings and shipped features. Assumptions: ~25 PTX agents handling ~80 actions each per day, highest-friction tasks cut ~40%.

What that means for the company

  • The freed capacity absorbs rising patient volume without adding PTX headcount, so support cost stays flat as the business grows.
  • Faster turnaround on orders and approvals means quicker responses for patients and pharmacies, supporting retention.
  • Bringing AP and SAS approvals into Circuit, out of side spreadsheets, cuts manual-handling errors and lowers compliance risk.
  • A consistent MUI design system makes every future change cheaper to build and quicker to ship.

Circuit admin redesign, Montu, 2024. Participants and admin screens de-identified to protect patient data.
